title: Israel Heads to First Post-October 7 Election With Netanyahu's Grip on Power in Doubt
excerpt: Israelis will vote on October 27 in a parliamentary election shaped by the Gaza war, with former military chief Gadi Eisenkot emerging as the prime minister's most serious challenger in years.
body:
• Israel's October 27 election will be the first since the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack, with polls showing Prime Minister Netanyahu on course to lose power.
  • Former IDF chief Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party has surged past the Bennett-Lapid alliance to become Netanyahu's primary rival, with recent polls placing him nearly level with Likud.
  • The 25th Knesset is completing its full four-year term for the first time since 1988, but Israel's fragmented proportional representation system means coalition-building will be decisive.
  • The outcome will shape the future of the Gaza conflict, Israeli-Arab relations, and broader Middle East stability — all issues with direct implications for Indian strategic interests in the region.

Israel is heading to the polls on October 27 in a parliamentary election that could mark the end of Benjamin Netanyahu's record-breaking tenure as prime minister. Shaped by the aftermath of the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack and the wars that followed in Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran, the vote will be the country's first national ballot since the deadliest day in its history.

Successive polls show Netanyahu's Likud party trailing or narrowly leading, while the prime minister's personal approval ratings have cratered. The October 7 attacks shattered his carefully cultivated security credentials, and voters have shown little faith in his wartime leadership despite broadly supporting the military operations themselves, according to Reuters.

How Israeli Elections Work

Israel's electoral system differs sharply from the constituency-based models familiar to Indian voters. The country uses closed-list proportional representation: citizens vote for a party, not an individual candidate. All 120 seats in the Knesset, Israel's parliament, are allocated nationally to parties that clear a 3.25% electoral threshold — equivalent to roughly four seats.

No single party in Israel has ever won an outright majority. Governments are formed through coalitions, giving small parties outsized leverage. The leader of the party that assembles a coalition commanding at least 61 seats becomes prime minister. This system has frequently produced fragile governments — between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five elections in under four years.

The current Knesset broke that pattern, serving its full four-year term for the first time since 1988. Parties must submit their candidate lists by September 9, and the political landscape could still shift before election day.

The Challengers: Eisenkot's Rise and a Fragmented Opposition

The most significant development has been the ascent of Gadi Eisenkot, a former IDF chief of staff who founded the Yashar ("honest" or "straight" in Hebrew) party less than a year ago. Initially polling in the single digits, Yashar has surged to become the leading opposition force. A Channel 12 poll in late June projected 21 seats for Yashar — just behind Likud's 23 and ahead of the 18 projected for Together, the alliance between former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid.

"There is only one Netanyahu. Eisenkot is the first in years who is trying to beat Netanyahu by being his opposite."

— Anshel Pfeffer, Israel correspondent for The Economist

Eisenkot, 66, is the son of Moroccan immigrants raised in Israel's geographic periphery — a sharp contrast to Netanyahu's elite Jerusalem upbringing and Ivy League polish. His personal story has resonated deeply: his youngest son Gal was killed fighting in Gaza in December 2023, along with two nephews. Meanwhile, Netanyahu's own son Yair spent much of the war in Miami.

Other key contenders include Avigdor Lieberman's Yisrael Beiteinu, which draws support from the ex-Soviet immigrant community; Benny Gantz's Blue and White party; the ultra-Orthodox Shas and United Torah Judaism parties; and left-wing Democrats led by former general Yair Golan. Four parties representing Israel's 20% Arab minority — Hadash, Taal, Raam, and Balad — are also contesting seats.

What's at Stake for the Middle East

The election's outcome will have consequences far beyond Israel's borders. The next government will inherit the unresolved Gaza conflict, a fragile ceasefire with Hezbollah in Lebanon, and a volatile relationship with Iran. Whether Israel pursues a diplomatic endgame or continues its current military-first approach depends heavily on who leads the next coalition.

Netanyahu's current coalition partners — Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich's Religious Zionism and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's far-right Jewish Power — have pushed expansionist policies in the West Bank that have drawn international condemnation. A change in government could recalibrate Israel's relationships with Arab states, the Palestinian Authority, and Western allies.

Coalition arithmetic remains the central challenge for the opposition. Even if polls point to a theoretical anti-Netanyahu majority, assembling a government spanning left, right, centre, and Arab parties would be difficult — and keeping it intact even harder. Bennett and Lapid's own multi-party government lasted only 18 months in 2021-2022.

Why It Matters for the Indian Diaspora

India and Israel share a robust defence and technology partnership that has deepened under the Modi-Netanyahu era. The election's outcome could reshape diplomatic dynamics that affect India's defence procurement, counterterrorism cooperation, and technology transfers. For the estimated 85,000 Indians living in Israel — including a significant community of caregivers and agricultural workers — the security situation and government policies on foreign workers carry direct personal stakes.

Looking Ahead

With nearly three months until election day, the race remains fluid. Netanyahu is a consummate political survivor who has overcome seemingly impossible odds before, and his Likud party retains a loyal base. But the convergence of the October 7 aftermath, personal corruption cases still winding through courts, and an energised challenger in Eisenkot has created the most serious threat to his hold on power in years.

"Eisenkot is not Netanyahu and can never be. But that may be precisely what many Israelis are looking for: a fundamentally different style of leadership."

— Anshel Pfeffer, The Economist

The September deadline for party list submissions will clarify the field, and potential mergers or dropouts could reshape the race. For now, Israel's election is shaping up as a referendum on Netanyahu's leadership in the aftermath of the country's most traumatic period since its founding.
